notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Natural resources are materials and environmental components obtained from nature and used by humans.
  • They include:
  • Land.
  • Water.
  • Soil.
  • Minerals.
  • Forests.
  • Wildlife.
  • Energy resources.
  • Natural resources differ greatly in their rate of formation and renewability.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Natural Resources → Renewable + Non-Renewable

2. Renewable Resources
  • Renewable resources can be replenished naturally within a relatively short period if used sustainably.
  • Examples include:
  • Solar energy.
  • Wind energy.
  • Flowing water.
  • Biomass.
  • Forest resources under sustainable management.
3. Non-Renewable Resources
  • Non-renewable resources form over extremely long geological periods.
  • Their stocks are finite on the human timescale.
  • Examples include:
  • Coal.
  • Petroleum.
  • Natural gas.
  • Metallic minerals.
  • Uranium.
📌 Must-Memorise

Coal + Petroleum + Natural Gas → Non-Renewable

4. Conventional Energy Sources

Conventional energy sources traditionally used on a large scale include:

  • Coal.
  • Petroleum.
  • Natural gas.
  • Hydroelectric power.
  • Traditional biomass.
5. Non-Conventional Energy Sources

Common non-conventional or alternative sources include:

  • Solar energy.
  • Wind energy.
  • Tidal energy.
  • Geothermal energy.
  • Biogas.
  • Modern biomass energy.
  • Ocean energy.
6. Commercial Energy

Commercial energy sources are bought and sold in markets.

Examples include:

  • Coal.
  • Petroleum.
  • Natural gas.
  • Electricity.
7. Non-Commercial Energy

Traditional non-commercial sources include:

  • Firewood.
  • Agricultural residues.
  • Animal dung used directly as fuel.

Their relative importance is higher in some rural areas.

8. Primary Energy
  • Primary energy is energy available directly from natural sources before conversion.
  • Examples:
  • Coal.
  • Crude oil.
  • Natural gas.
  • Sunlight.
  • Wind.
  • Flowing water.
9. Secondary Energy
  • Secondary energy is produced by converting primary energy.
  • Examples:
  • Electricity.
  • Petrol.
  • Diesel.
  • Hydrogen produced from another energy source.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Electricity → Secondary Energy, not a Primary Natural Resource

10. Fossil Fuels

Major fossil fuels are:

  • Coal.
  • Petroleum.
  • Natural gas.

They formed from ancient organic matter over geological time.

11. Coal — Basic Facts
  • Coal is a combustible sedimentary organic rock.
  • It formed mainly from ancient plant material buried and transformed under heat and pressure.
  • Coal is a major conventional energy resource.
  • It is also an important industrial raw material.
12. Coalification
  • Coalification is the gradual transformation of plant material into coal.
  • Increasing heat, pressure and time generally increase carbon content.
13. Main Ranks of Coal

From lower to higher carbon content:

  • Peat.
  • Lignite.
  • Bituminous coal.
  • Anthracite.
📌 Must-Memorise

Peat → Lignite → Bituminous → Anthracite

14. Peat
  • Peat is an early stage in coal formation.
  • It contains high moisture and relatively low carbon.
  • It produces less heat than higher-rank coal.
15. Lignite
  • Lignite is commonly called brown coal.
  • It contains more carbon than peat but less than bituminous coal.
  • It has relatively high moisture content.
  • It is widely used for electricity generation near mining areas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lignite → Brown Coal

16. Bituminous Coal
  • Bituminous coal has higher carbon and calorific value than lignite.
  • It is the most important commercial coal type in many Indian coalfields.
  • Certain bituminous varieties are suitable for making coke.
17. Anthracite
  • Anthracite has the highest carbon content among the major coal ranks.
  • It is hard and has high calorific value.
  • Indian reserves of high-quality anthracite are limited.
📌 Must-Memorise

Highest Grade Coal → Anthracite

18. Coking Coal
  • Coking coal can be converted into coke by heating in the absence of air.
  • Coke is essential in conventional blast-furnace iron and steel production.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Coking Coal → Coke → Iron and Steel

19. Non-Coking Coal
  • Non-coking coal is mainly used for:
  • Thermal power.
  • Cement.
  • Industrial boilers.
  • It does not possess the required coking properties for metallurgical coke.
20. Geological Coal Groups in India

India's coal deposits are broadly associated with:

  • Gondwana coal.
  • Tertiary coal.
21. Gondwana Coal
  • Gondwana coal deposits are much older than Tertiary coal.
  • They occur mainly in Peninsular river valleys.
  • They contain the bulk of India's major coalfields.
📌 Must-Memorise

Major Indian Coal → Gondwana

22. Major Gondwana Coal Valleys

Important coal-bearing river valleys include:

  • Damodar.
  • Son.
  • Mahanadi.
  • Godavari.
  • Wardha.
23. Damodar Valley Coalfields

Important coalfields include:

  • Jharia.
  • Bokaro.
  • Giridih.
  • Raniganj.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Damodar Valley → Major Coal Belt

24. Jharia Coalfield
  • Jharia lies in Jharkhand.
  • It is famous for high-quality coking coal.
  • It has historically supplied the iron and steel industry.
  • Underground mine fires are a major environmental problem.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jharia → Coking Coal → Jharkhand

25. Bokaro Coalfield
  • Bokaro lies in Jharkhand.
  • It forms part of the Damodar Valley coal belt.
26. Giridih Coalfield
  • Giridih is another important coalfield of Jharkhand.
  • It is historically associated with good-quality coal.
27. Raniganj Coalfield
  • Raniganj lies mainly in West Bengal.
  • It is one of India's oldest commercially exploited coalfields.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Raniganj → West Bengal → Historic Coalfield

28. Son Valley Coal
  • Coalfields occur in the Son basin and adjoining central Indian regions.
  • Important deposits extend through Madhya Pradesh and adjoining states.
29. Singrauli Coalfield
  • Singrauli lies across parts of Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
  • It is a major coal and thermal-power region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Singrauli → Coal + Thermal Power

30. Korba Coalfield
  • Korba lies in Chhattisgarh.
  • It is a major coal-producing and thermal-power region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Korba → Coal → Chhattisgarh

31. Talcher Coalfield
  • Talcher is an important coalfield in Odisha.
  • It lies in the Mahanadi basin.
📌 Must-Memorise

Talcher → Coal → Odisha

32. Ib Valley Coalfield
  • Ib Valley is another important coal-bearing region of Odisha.
33. Godavari Valley Coalfields
  • Coal deposits occur in the Godavari Valley.
  • Telangana contains important coalfields in this basin.
34. Singareni Coalfields
  • Singareni coalfields lie in Telangana.
  • They are associated with the Godavari Valley coal belt.
📌 Must-Memorise

Singareni → Coal → Telangana

35. Wardha Valley Coal
  • Coalfields also occur in the Wardha Valley of Maharashtra.
  • They form part of the Gondwana coal system.
36. Tertiary Coal
  • Tertiary coal is geologically younger.
  • It occurs mainly in northeastern India and selected Himalayan regions.
  • Deposits occur in states such as:
  • Assam.
  • Meghalaya.
  • Nagaland.
  • Arunachal Pradesh.
37. Coal in Northeast India
  • Northeastern coal may contain relatively high sulphur in some deposits.
  • Mining occurs in structurally complex hill terrain.
38. Lignite Deposits of India

Important lignite regions include:

  • Neyveli in Tamil Nadu.
  • Rajasthan.
  • Gujarat.
  • Other smaller sedimentary basins.
39. Neyveli Lignite
  • Neyveli lies in Cuddalore district of Tamil Nadu.
  • It is India's best-known lignite field.
  • Lignite is used mainly for thermal-power generation.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Neyveli → Lignite → Cuddalore

40. Why Thermal Plants Often Lie Near Coalfields
  • Coal is bulky.
  • Transporting large quantities is expensive.
  • Locating thermal plants near mines reduces transport costs.
  • Large water supplies are also required for cooling and steam generation.
41. Thermal Power
  • Thermal power plants generate electricity using heat.
  • Fossil-fuel thermal plants commonly burn:
  • Coal.
  • Lignite.
  • Natural gas.
  • Heat converts water into steam, which drives turbines.
42. Coal-Based Thermal Power Problems

Major environmental issues include:

  • Carbon dioxide emissions.
  • Sulphur oxides.
  • Nitrogen oxides.
  • Particulate pollution.
  • Fly ash.
  • Water use.
  • Mining impacts.
43. Fly Ash
  • Fly ash is fine particulate residue produced during coal combustion.
  • It can be used in:
  • Cement.
  • Bricks.
  • Road construction.
  • Poor disposal can pollute land, air and water.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Coal Power Waste → Fly Ash

44. Petroleum — Basic Facts
  • Petroleum is a liquid fossil fuel.
  • It consists mainly of hydrocarbons.
  • It forms from buried organic matter subjected to heat and pressure over geological time.
  • Crude petroleum is refined into many useful products.
45. Meaning of Petroleum
  • Petroleum literally means "rock oil."
  • It occurs in sedimentary basins.
46. Petroleum Formation

Petroleum generally forms where:

  • Organic-rich sediments accumulate.
  • Burial increases temperature and pressure.
  • Hydrocarbons migrate from source rocks.
  • Reservoir rocks trap them beneath impermeable cap rocks.
47. Source Rock
  • Source rock contains organic material from which petroleum or natural gas forms.
  • Fine-grained sedimentary rocks such as shale can serve as source rocks.
48. Reservoir Rock
  • Reservoir rock is porous and permeable.
  • It stores oil or natural gas.
  • Sandstone and limestone can act as reservoir rocks.
49. Cap Rock
  • Cap rock is an impermeable layer that prevents hydrocarbons from escaping upward.
  • Shale or salt layers may form effective cap rocks.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Petroleum Trap → Source + Reservoir + Cap Rock

50. Oil Trap

Common geological traps include:

  • Anticline traps.
  • Fault traps.
  • Stratigraphic traps.
  • Salt-dome-related traps.
51. Anticline
  • An anticline is an upward arch in rock layers.
  • Oil and gas may accumulate beneath impermeable rock near the crest.
52. Major Petroleum Regions of India

Traditional petroleum-producing regions include:

  • Assam.
  • Gujarat.
  • Mumbai Offshore.
  • Krishna-Godavari Basin.
  • Cauvery Basin.
  • Rajasthan.
53. Digboi
  • Digboi is in Assam.
  • It is one of India's oldest petroleum-producing centres.
  • It became historically famous for oil production and refining.
📌 Must-Memorise

Digboi → Petroleum → Assam

54. Naharkatiya
  • Naharkatiya is an important oilfield in Assam.
55. Moran
  • Moran is another petroleum-producing region of Assam.
56. Gujarat Petroleum

Important oil-producing regions include:

  • Ankleshwar.
  • Kalol.
  • Mehsana and adjoining basins.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ankleshwar → Petroleum → Gujarat

57. Ankleshwar
  • Ankleshwar is one of Gujarat's important petroleum fields.
  • It lies in the Cambay basin region.
58. Mumbai High
  • Mumbai High is a major offshore petroleum field in the Arabian Sea.
  • It lies west of Mumbai.
  • It is located on the continental shelf.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mumbai High → Offshore Oil → Arabian Sea

59. Offshore Oil
  • Offshore petroleum is extracted from beneath the seabed.
  • Platforms and subsea wells are used.
  • Extraction requires specialised technology.
60. Krishna-Godavari Basin
  • The Krishna-Godavari Basin lies along the eastern coast.
  • It contains important petroleum and natural-gas resources.
  • Both onshore and offshore deposits occur.
📌 Must-Memorise

KG Basin → Oil + Natural Gas

61. Cauvery Basin
  • The Cauvery sedimentary basin extends across parts of Tamil Nadu and adjoining offshore areas.
  • It contains petroleum and natural-gas resources.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Cauvery Basin → Tamil Nadu Oil and Gas Region

62. Rajasthan Petroleum
  • Western Rajasthan contains important hydrocarbon-bearing sedimentary basins.
  • The Barmer region is especially significant for petroleum.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Barmer → Petroleum → Rajasthan

63. Petroleum Refining
  • Crude oil cannot be used directly for most purposes.
  • Refineries separate and process it into useful products.
64. Fractional Distillation
  • Petroleum refining uses differences in boiling points.
  • Fractional distillation separates hydrocarbon fractions.
65. Major Petroleum Products

Important products include:

  • LPG.
  • Petrol.
  • Naphtha.
  • Kerosene.
  • Aviation turbine fuel.
  • Diesel.
  • Lubricants.
  • Paraffin wax.
  • Bitumen.
66. Petrol
  • Petrol is a light petroleum fraction.
  • It is widely used in spark-ignition engines.
67. Diesel
  • Diesel is a heavier fuel than petrol.
  • It is used in compression-ignition engines and several industrial applications.
68. LPG
  • LPG means Liquefied Petroleum Gas.
  • It consists mainly of propane and butane.
  • It is stored under pressure in liquid form.
📌 Must-Memorise

LPG → Mainly Propane + Butane

69. Bitumen
  • Bitumen is a heavy petroleum product.
  • It is widely used in road construction and waterproofing.
70. Petrochemicals

Petroleum and natural gas provide feedstock for:

  • Plastics.
  • Synthetic fibres.
  • Fertilisers.
  • Detergents.
  • Solvents.
  • Synthetic rubber.
71. Natural Gas — Basic Facts
  • Natural gas is a gaseous fossil fuel.
  • Methane is its principal component.
  • It may occur:
  • With petroleum.
  • Independently in gas fields.
  • It burns more cleanly than coal in terms of many air pollutants.
📌 Must-Memorise

Natural Gas → Mainly Methane

72. Associated Gas
  • Associated natural gas occurs together with crude oil in petroleum reservoirs.
73. Non-Associated Gas
  • Non-associated gas occurs in reservoirs containing mainly natural gas rather than crude oil.
74. Major Natural Gas Regions

Important regions include:

  • Mumbai Offshore.
  • Krishna-Godavari Basin.
  • Assam.
  • Gujarat.
  • Tripura.
  • Cauvery Basin.
  • Rajasthan.
75. Natural Gas Uses

Natural gas is used for:

  • Electricity generation.
  • Fertiliser production.
  • Industrial heating.
  • Domestic cooking.
  • Transport fuel.
  • Petrochemicals.
76. CNG
  • CNG means Compressed Natural Gas.
  • It is natural gas stored at high pressure.
  • It is used as vehicle fuel.
📌 Must-Memorise

CNG → Compressed Natural Gas

77. PNG
  • PNG means Piped Natural Gas.
  • It is supplied through pipelines to homes, commercial establishments and industries.
78. LNG
  • LNG means Liquefied Natural Gas.
  • Natural gas is cooled to very low temperature and converted into liquid.
  • Liquefaction greatly reduces its volume for transport.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

LNG → Natural Gas Liquefied for Transport

79. Gas Pipelines
  • Pipelines transport natural gas efficiently over long distances.
  • They connect:
  • Gas fields.
  • LNG terminals.
  • Fertiliser plants.
  • Power plants.
  • Cities.
80. Hydroelectric Power — Basic Principle
  • Hydroelectric power uses the energy of flowing or falling water.
  • Water turns turbines.
  • Turbines drive generators to produce electricity.
81. Hydropower as Renewable Energy
  • Hydropower is generally classified as renewable because the water cycle is continuously renewed.
  • However, large dams can have major ecological and social impacts.
82. Conditions Favourable for Hydropower

Important conditions include:

  • Large water discharge.
  • Steep gradient.
  • Suitable dam site.
  • Narrow valley.
  • Strong foundation rock.
  • Reliable rainfall or snowmelt.
83. Himalayan Hydropower
  • Himalayan rivers have high hydropower potential because of:
  • Steep slopes.
  • Large discharge.
  • Deep valleys.
84. Peninsular Hydropower
  • Western Ghats and plateau rivers also provide important hydropower sites.
  • Waterfalls and escarpments create significant hydraulic head.
85. Multipurpose Projects

Hydroelectric projects may also provide:

  • Irrigation.
  • Drinking water.
  • Flood control.
  • Fisheries.
  • Reservoir storage.
86. Major Hydropower Project Pairings

Examples include:

  • Bhakra → Sutlej.
  • Tehri → Bhagirathi.
  • Hirakud → Mahanadi.
  • Sardar Sarovar → Narmada.
  • Nagarjuna Sagar → Krishna.
  • Mettur → Kaveri system functions including power and irrigation.
87. Pumped-Storage Hydropower
  • Pumped storage moves water from a lower reservoir to a higher reservoir when excess electricity is available.
  • Water is released later to generate electricity during high demand.
  • It functions as large-scale energy storage.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

Pumped Storage → Electricity Storage Using Water

88. Solar Energy
  • Solar energy comes from solar radiation.
  • India receives abundant sunlight because of its tropical and subtropical location.
  • Solar energy can be converted into:
  • Electricity.
  • Heat.
89. Solar Photovoltaic Energy
  • Photovoltaic cells directly convert sunlight into electricity.
  • They are commonly called solar cells.
📌 Must-Memorise

Photovoltaic Cell → Sunlight Directly to Electricity

90. Solar Thermal Energy
  • Solar thermal systems use solar radiation to produce heat.
  • Applications include:
  • Water heating.
  • Cooking.
  • Industrial heating.
  • Electricity generation in concentrated systems.
91. Solar Energy Potential Regions

High solar-energy potential occurs especially in:

  • Rajasthan.
  • Gujarat.
  • Interior Deccan.
  • Dry regions with high sunshine.
92. Advantages of Solar Energy
  • Renewable.
  • No direct fuel cost.
  • Low operational emissions.
  • Suitable for decentralised supply.
  • Useful in remote regions.
93. Limitations of Solar Energy
  • Intermittent.
  • Depends on daylight and weather.
  • Requires land for large projects.
  • Requires storage or grid balancing.
  • Manufacturing and disposal of panels have environmental impacts.
94. Rooftop Solar
  • Rooftop solar generates electricity close to where it is consumed.
  • It can reduce transmission losses and land requirements.
95. Floating Solar
  • Floating photovoltaic systems are installed on reservoirs and other water bodies.
  • They reduce land requirement.
  • They may also reduce some surface evaporation.
96. Wind Energy — Basic Principle
  • Wind turbines convert kinetic energy of moving air into electricity.
  • Wind turns turbine blades.
  • A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
97. Conditions for Wind Power

Wind-energy sites require:

  • Strong winds.
  • Reliable wind regime.
  • Open terrain or mountain passes.
  • Grid connectivity.
  • Suitable land.
98. Major Wind-Potential Regions of India

Important wind-energy regions include:

  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Gujarat.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Karnataka.
  • Rajasthan.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
99. Tamil Nadu Wind Energy
  • Tamil Nadu has major wind-energy resources.
  • Southern and western parts of the state contain important wind corridors.
  • Mountain gaps help channel strong winds.
100. Muppandal
  • Muppandal in Kanyakumari district is one of Tamil Nadu's best-known wind-energy locations.
  • Strong winds are channelled through the southern Western Ghats region.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Muppandal → Wind Energy → Kanyakumari

101. Palghat Gap and Wind
  • Palghat Gap channels winds between Kerala and western Tamil Nadu.
  • Areas around Coimbatore and Tiruppur benefit from favourable wind conditions.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Palghat Gap → Western Tamil Nadu Wind Corridor

102. Kayathar
  • Kayathar in southern Tamil Nadu is another important wind-energy region.
  • It lies in the Thoothukudi district area.
103. Advantages of Wind Energy
  • Renewable.
  • No fuel combustion.
  • Low operational emissions.
  • Land beneath turbines may still support some agriculture or grazing.
104. Limitations of Wind Energy
  • Intermittent.
  • Site-specific.
  • Requires grid management.
  • Can affect birds and bats if poorly located.
  • Visual and noise impacts may occur locally.
105. Biomass Energy
  • Biomass energy comes from recently living organic material.
  • Sources include:
  • Crop residues.
  • Wood.
  • Animal waste.
  • Organic municipal waste.
  • Energy crops.
106. Biomass vs Fossil Fuel
  • Biomass is part of the relatively short-term biological carbon cycle.
  • Fossil fuels contain carbon stored underground over geological time.
  • Unsustainable biomass use can still cause deforestation and pollution.
107. Biogas
  • Biogas is produced by anaerobic decomposition of organic matter.
  • It contains mainly:
  • Methane.
  • Carbon dioxide.
📌 Must-Memorise

Biogas → Anaerobic Digestion → Methane

108. Anaerobic Digestion
  • Anaerobic digestion occurs without oxygen.
  • Microorganisms break down organic matter and produce biogas.
109. Biogas Feedstock

Common feedstocks include:

  • Cattle dung.
  • Food waste.
  • Sewage sludge.
  • Agricultural waste.
110. Benefits of Biogas
  • Provides cooking or power fuel.
  • Reduces organic waste.
  • Produces nutrient-rich slurry usable as manure.
  • Reduces direct burning of biomass.
111. Bagasse
  • Bagasse is fibrous residue left after extracting juice from sugarcane.
  • It is used as fuel in sugar mills.
  • It can generate both heat and electricity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bagasse → Sugarcane Waste → Energy

112. Cogeneration
  • Cogeneration means simultaneous production of electricity and useful heat.
  • Sugar mills commonly use bagasse-based cogeneration.
113. Biofuels

Biofuels include:

  • Ethanol.
  • Biodiesel.
  • Biogas.
  • Other fuels derived from biomass.
114. Ethanol
  • Ethanol is an alcohol fuel.
  • It can be produced from:
  • Sugarcane products.
  • Grains.
  • Other biomass feedstocks.
  • It can be blended with petrol.
115. Biodiesel
  • Biodiesel can be produced from vegetable oils, used cooking oils and certain other biological feedstocks.
  • It can substitute partly for petroleum diesel.
116. Waste-to-Energy
  • Waste-to-energy uses suitable waste streams to produce:
  • Electricity.
  • Heat.
  • Biogas.
  • Waste segregation is essential for efficient and environmentally sound operation.
117. Geothermal Energy
  • Geothermal energy is heat from within the Earth.
  • Hot water and steam from underground can be used for heating or electricity generation.
118. Geothermal Regions of India

Important geothermal areas include:

  • Puga Valley in Ladakh.
  • Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh.
  • Tattapani region.
  • Several hot-spring belts.
📌 Must-Memorise

Puga Valley → Geothermal → Ladakh

119. Hot Springs
  • Hot springs occur where groundwater is heated underground and returns to the surface.
  • They may be associated with faults and geothermal gradients.
120. Tidal Energy
  • Tidal energy uses the periodic rise and fall or movement of seawater caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun.
  • It is predictable but geographically restricted.
121. Tidal Energy Potential in India

Areas often identified for tidal-energy potential include:

  • Gulf of Kachchh.
  • Gulf of Khambhat.
  • Sundarbans region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tidal Potential → Kachchh + Khambhat

122. Wave Energy
  • Wave energy uses energy from ocean surface waves.
  • It differs from tidal energy.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Wave Energy ≠ Tidal Energy

123. Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion
  • OTEC uses the temperature difference between warm surface ocean water and colder deep ocean water.
  • Tropical oceans provide favourable conditions where temperature differences are sufficient.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

OTEC → Warm Surface Water + Cold Deep Water

124. Hydrogen Energy
  • Hydrogen is an energy carrier rather than a primary energy source.
  • It can be produced using several methods.
  • When used in a fuel cell, hydrogen can generate electricity.
125. Green Hydrogen
  • Green hydrogen is produced by electrolysis using renewable electricity.
  • Water is split into hydrogen and oxygen.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Green Hydrogen → Renewable Electricity + Electrolysis

126. Fuel Cell
  • A fuel cell converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy.
  • Hydrogen fuel cells produce water as a major reaction product.
127. Nuclear Energy
  • Nuclear power uses energy released from atomic nuclei.
  • Commercial nuclear reactors primarily use nuclear fission.
128. Nuclear Fission
  • Nuclear fission is splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus.
  • It releases large amounts of energy.
  • Uranium is an important nuclear fuel.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fission → Splitting Heavy Nucleus

129. Nuclear Fusion
  • Nuclear fusion combines light nuclei.
  • It powers the Sun and stars.
  • Controlled commercial fusion remains technologically challenging.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Sun's Energy → Nuclear Fusion, not Fission

130. Uranium
  • Uranium is a radioactive metallic element.
  • Uranium-235 is fissile and can sustain a nuclear chain reaction.
  • India has uranium deposits in several geological regions.
131. Important Uranium Regions

Examples include:

  • Jaduguda → Jharkhand.
  • Tummalapalle → Andhra Pradesh.
  • Other deposits occur in several states.
132. Thorium
  • Thorium is a radioactive element.
  • India has significant thorium-bearing monazite in coastal sands.
  • Thorium-232 is fertile rather than directly fissile in the usual reactor sense.
📌 Must-Memorise

Thorium → Monazite Beach Sands

133. Monazite
  • Monazite occurs in heavy-mineral coastal sands.
  • It contains:
  • Thorium.
  • Rare-earth elements.
  • Important deposits occur along parts of Kerala, Tamil Nadu and other coasts.
134. Tamil Nadu and Atomic Minerals
  • Southern Tamil Nadu's coastal sands contain monazite and other heavy minerals.
  • Kanyakumari, Tirunelveli and Thoothukudi coastal sectors are important geographically.
135. Nuclear Power Plant Locations — Geography Awareness

Important nuclear-power locations include:

  • Tarapur → Maharashtra.
  • Rawatbhata → Rajasthan.
  • Narora → Uttar Pradesh.
  • Kakrapar → Gujarat.
  • Kaiga → Karnataka.
  • Kalpakkam → Tamil Nadu.
  • Kudankulam → Tamil Nadu.
136. Kalpakkam
  • Kalpakkam lies on the Tamil Nadu coast south of Chennai.
  • It is an important nuclear-energy centre.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Kalpakkam → Nuclear Energy → Tamil Nadu

137. Kudankulam
  • Kudankulam lies in Tirunelveli district region of southern Tamil Nadu.
  • It is an important nuclear-power location.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Kudankulam → Nuclear Power → Tirunelveli

138. Advantages of Nuclear Power
  • Very high energy density.
  • Low direct carbon dioxide emissions during electricity generation.
  • Large continuous power output is possible.
139. Challenges of Nuclear Power
  • Radioactive waste.
  • High capital cost.
  • Safety requirements.
  • Decommissioning.
  • Uranium fuel-cycle management.
140. Radioactive Waste
  • Radioactive waste remains hazardous for varying periods.
  • Safe containment, storage and disposal are essential.
141. Energy Resource Distribution and Industry

Industries develop in relation to energy availability.

Examples:

  • Aluminium → Cheap electricity.
  • Iron and steel → Coal/coke historically important.
  • Petrochemicals → Petroleum and natural gas.
  • Fertilisers → Natural gas as important feedstock.
142. Energy Security
  • Energy security means reliable and affordable access to sufficient energy.
  • It depends on:
  • Domestic resources.
  • Imports.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Diversification.
  • Storage.
  • Efficiency.
143. Energy Mix
  • Energy mix means the combination of different energy sources used by a country or region.
  • Diversification reduces dependence on a single resource.
144. Energy Conservation

Energy conservation means reducing unnecessary energy use.

Methods include:

  • Efficient appliances.
  • Public transport.
  • Better industrial processes.
  • Efficient buildings.
  • Reduced transmission losses.
145. Energy Efficiency
  • Energy efficiency means obtaining the same service with less energy.
  • It differs from simply reducing activity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Efficiency → Same Output with Less Energy

146. Renewable Energy and Storage
  • Solar and wind output varies with weather and time.
  • Storage helps balance supply and demand.
  • Storage options include:
  • Batteries.
  • Pumped hydropower.
  • Hydrogen.
147. Grid
  • An electricity grid is an interconnected network of:
  • Generating stations.
  • Transmission lines.
  • Substations.
  • Distribution networks.
148. Transmission
  • Transmission carries electricity over long distances at high voltage.
  • High voltage reduces energy loss for a given power transfer.
149. Distribution
  • Distribution delivers electricity from substations to consumers.
150. Decentralised Energy
  • Decentralised systems generate energy close to users.
  • Examples include:
  • Rooftop solar.
  • Village biogas.
  • Small hydro.
  • They can benefit remote regions.
151. Small Hydropower
  • Small hydropower uses smaller rivers or canal drops.
  • It generally has smaller reservoirs and localised impacts than very large dams, although environmental effects still require assessment.
152. Run-of-River Hydropower
  • Run-of-river plants use river flow with limited storage compared with large reservoir projects.
  • They still alter river flow and ecology locally.
153. Other Natural Resources — Forest Biomass
  • Forests supply:
  • Timber.
  • Fuelwood.
  • Fodder.
  • Medicinal plants.
  • Non-timber forest products.
  • Forest resources must be managed sustainably.

Detailed forest geography follows in the next chapter.

154. Water as an Energy Resource
  • Flowing water provides hydropower.
  • Water is also essential for:
  • Thermal power cooling.
  • Nuclear power cooling.
  • Biofuel production.
  • Energy and water systems are therefore interconnected.
155. Land-Energy Link

Energy development requires land for:

  • Coal mines.
  • Oil installations.
  • Solar parks.
  • Wind farms.
  • Transmission lines.
  • Reservoirs.

Energy planning therefore affects land resources.

156. Mining-Energy Link

Coal, uranium and petroleum extraction can cause:

  • Habitat loss.
  • Land degradation.
  • Water pollution.
  • Community displacement.
  • Air pollution.
157. Fossil Fuels and Greenhouse Gases
  • Burning coal, petroleum and natural gas releases carbon dioxide.
  • Fossil-fuel combustion is a major source of anthropogenic greenhouse-gas emissions.
158. Coal vs Natural Gas

Coal:

  • Solid.
  • Higher particulate and ash problems.
  • High carbon emissions.

Natural gas:

  • Gaseous.
  • Mainly methane.
  • Burns with lower carbon dioxide emissions per unit of energy than coal, but methane leakage can reduce climate benefits.
159. Petroleum vs Natural Gas

Petroleum:

  • Liquid hydrocarbons.
  • Major transport fuel source.

Natural gas:

  • Mainly methane.
  • Used in power, fertiliser, industry and households.
160. Renewable vs Non-Renewable Energy

Renewable:

  • Solar.
  • Wind.
  • Hydropower.
  • Biomass.
  • Geothermal.

Non-renewable:

  • Coal.
  • Petroleum.
  • Natural gas.
  • Uranium.
161. Tamil Nadu — Energy Geography Overview

Important energy resources and locations include:

  • Neyveli → Lignite.
  • Cauvery Basin → Oil and natural gas.
  • Muppandal → Wind.
  • Kayathar → Wind.
  • Western Tamil Nadu → Major wind corridors.
  • Kalpakkam → Nuclear energy.
  • Kudankulam → Nuclear energy.
  • Hydropower → Western Ghats.
  • Solar energy → Dry interior and southern regions.
162. Neyveli
  • Neyveli is located in Cuddalore district.
  • It is associated with:
  • Lignite mining.
  • Thermal power.
  • It is one of Tamil Nadu's most important energy-resource centres.
163. Cauvery Basin Hydrocarbons
  • The Cauvery Basin contains sedimentary formations with petroleum and natural gas.
  • Hydrocarbon-bearing regions occur both onshore and offshore.
164. Narimanam
  • Narimanam in the Cauvery delta region is associated with petroleum production in Tamil Nadu.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Narimanam → Petroleum → Cauvery Basin

165. Manali Refinery Region
  • Chennai's northern industrial region around Manali is associated with petroleum refining and petrochemical industries.
  • Its coastal location supports crude-oil transport and industrial development.
166. Western Ghats Hydropower in Tamil Nadu
  • High rainfall and steep gradients in the Western Ghats favour hydropower.
  • Important hydroelectric regions occur in:
  • Nilgiris.
  • Anaimalai.
  • Southern Western Ghats.
167. Kundah Hydroelectric System
  • Kundah is an important hydroelectric region in the Nilgiris of Tamil Nadu.
  • High elevation and water storage support generation.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Kundah → Hydroelectricity → Nilgiris

168. Pykara
  • Pykara in the Nilgiris is historically associated with hydroelectric development.
  • The Pykara River and reservoirs support power generation.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Pykara → Hydropower → Nilgiris

169. Mettur Power Link
  • The Mettur project on Kaveri is associated with irrigation and hydroelectric generation.
  • Stanley Reservoir stores Kaveri water.
170. Tamil Nadu Solar Geography

High solar potential is favoured by:

  • Strong sunlight.
  • Dry conditions.
  • Large open areas.

Interior southern and western districts provide suitable locations for solar projects.

171. Kamuthi Solar Region
  • Kamuthi in Ramanathapuram district is widely associated with large-scale solar-power development.
  • The dry southern Tamil Nadu climate provides high solar radiation.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Kamuthi → Solar Energy → Ramanathapuram

172. Tamil Nadu Biomass Resources

Potential biomass sources include:

  • Sugarcane bagasse.
  • Rice husk.
  • Agricultural residues.
  • Animal waste.
  • Organic municipal waste.
173. Sugarcane Bagasse in Tamil Nadu
  • Sugar mills can use bagasse for cogeneration.
  • This converts an agricultural residue into electricity and useful heat.
174. Rice Husk
  • Rice husk is a by-product of rice milling.
  • It can be burned or converted into energy using suitable technologies.
175. Tamil Nadu Energy Advantages

The state has geographic access to diverse energy sources:

  • Lignite.
  • Wind.
  • Solar.
  • Hydropower.
  • Nuclear.
  • Oil and natural gas.
  • Biomass.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tamil Nadu → Highly Diversified Energy Geography

176. Resource Conservation

Natural-resource conservation requires:

  • Efficient use.
  • Recycling.
  • Pollution control.
  • Ecosystem restoration.
  • Sustainable extraction.
  • Renewable-energy development.
177. Circular Economy
  • A circular economy aims to keep materials in use for longer.
  • It promotes:
  • Reuse.
  • Repair.
  • Recycling.
  • Recovery.
  • It reduces pressure on natural resources.
178. Resource Efficiency
  • Resource efficiency means producing more value with less use of raw materials, water and energy.
179. Sustainable Resource Use

Sustainable use means meeting present needs without undermining the ability of future generations to meet their needs.

180. TNPSC High-Yield Pairings
  • Anthracite → Highest coal rank.
  • Lignite → Brown coal.
  • Jharia → Coking coal.
  • Raniganj → West Bengal.
  • Singareni → Telangana.

  • Korba → Chhattisgarh.

  • KG Basin → Oil and gas.
  • Cauvery Basin → Tamil Nadu hydrocarbons.
  • Natural gas → Methane.
  • LPG → Propane + Butane.
  • CNG → Compressed Natural Gas.
  • Solar cell → Photovoltaic.
  • Muppandal → Wind.
  • Puga → Geothermal.
  • Kachchh/Khambhat → Tidal potential.
  • Bagasse → Sugarcane residue.
  • Biogas → Methane.
  • Jaduguda → Uranium.
  • Monazite → Thorium.

  • Kundah → Hydropower.
  • Kamuthi → Solar.
181. TNPSC Traps
  • Renewable does not mean impact-free.
  • Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels.
  • Peat is lower rank than lignite.
  • Anthracite has the highest carbon content among major coal ranks.
  • Lignite is brown coal.
  • Jharia is famous for coking coal.
  • Raniganj is in West Bengal.
  • Singareni is in Telangana.
  • Neyveli is in Tamil Nadu.
  • Petroleum occurs mainly in sedimentary basins.
  • Digboi is in Assam.
  • Mumbai High is offshore in the Arabian Sea.
  • KG Basin is on the eastern side of peninsular India.
  • Cauvery Basin contains oil and gas.
  • Natural gas is mainly methane.
  • LPG is mainly propane and butane.
  • CNG and LNG are not the same.
  • Hydropower is renewable but large dams can have major impacts.
  • Photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly to electricity.
  • Wind power depends strongly on location.
  • Muppandal is associated with wind power.
  • Bagasse comes from sugarcane.
  • Biogas is produced anaerobically.
  • Puga Valley is associated with geothermal energy.
  • Tidal and wave energy are different.
  • Hydrogen is an energy carrier, not a primary natural source.
  • Green hydrogen uses renewable electricity.
  • Nuclear fission is used in nuclear power plants.
  • Nuclear fusion powers the Sun.
  • Uranium and thorium are not the same nuclear resource.
  • Monazite is associated with thorium.
  • Kalpakkam and Kudankulam are in Tamil Nadu.
  • Electricity is secondary energy.

  • Non-renewable → Coal/Oil/Gas.

  • Cauvery Basin → TN oil/gas.

  • Biogas → Methane.
  • Puga → Geothermal.
  • Kachchh → Tidal.
  • Fission → Nuclear power.
  • Fusion → Sun.
  • Jaduguda → Uranium.
  • Monazite → Thorium.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What are renewable resources? → Resources naturally replenished on a relatively short timescale.
  • Examples of renewable energy? → Solar, wind, hydropower, biomass and geothermal.
  • Examples of non-renewable energy? → Coal, petroleum, natural gas and uranium.
  • Three major fossil fuels? → Coal, petroleum and natural gas.
  • What is primary energy? → Energy available directly from natural sources.
  • Is electricity primary or secondary energy? → Secondary energy.
  • What is coalification? → Transformation of plant material into coal.
  • Correct coal-rank order? → Peat, lignite, bituminous, anthracite.
  • Brown coal? → Lignite.
  • Highest coal rank? → Anthracite.
  • Coal suitable for producing metallurgical coke? → Coking coal.
  • Main geological coal group of Peninsular India? → Gondwana coal.
  • Major coal valley in Jharkhand-West Bengal? → Damodar Valley.
  • Jharia is famous for? → Coking coal.
  • Raniganj lies in? → West Bengal.
  • Singrauli is associated with? → Coal and thermal power.
  • Korba lies in? → Chhattisgarh.
  • Talcher coalfield lies in? → Odisha.
  • Singareni coalfields lie in? → Telangana.
  • Important Tamil Nadu lignite centre? → Neyveli.
  • Neyveli lies in which district? → Cuddalore.
  • Major waste from coal thermal power? → Fly ash.
  • What is petroleum? → Liquid fossil fuel composed mainly of hydrocarbons.
  • Petroleum mainly occurs in what kind of rocks? → Sedimentary basins.
  • What is reservoir rock? → Porous, permeable rock that stores hydrocarbons.
  • What is cap rock? → Impermeable layer trapping hydrocarbons.
  • Old petroleum centre of Assam? → Digboi.
  • Important Gujarat oilfield? → Ankleshwar.
  • Major offshore oilfield west of Mumbai? → Mumbai High.
  • Major east-coast oil-gas basin? → Krishna-Godavari Basin.
  • Important Tamil Nadu hydrocarbon basin? → Cauvery Basin.
  • Barmer petroleum field lies in? → Rajasthan.
  • LPG full form? → Liquefied Petroleum Gas.
  • Main gases in LPG? → Propane and butane.
  • Main component of natural gas? → Methane.
  • CNG full form? → Compressed Natural Gas.
  • PNG full form? → Piped Natural Gas.
  • LNG full form? → Liquefied Natural Gas.
  • Main principle of hydropower? → Falling or flowing water turns turbines.
  • Why are Himalayas favourable for hydropower? → Steep gradients and large river discharge.
  • What is pumped-storage hydropower? → Water is pumped uphill and later released to generate electricity.
  • What does a photovoltaic cell do? → Converts sunlight directly into electricity.
  • High solar-potential regions of India? → Rajasthan, Gujarat and dry interior regions.
  • What converts wind into electricity? → Wind turbine.
  • Famous Tamil Nadu wind-energy centre? → Muppandal.
  • Muppandal is in? → Kanyakumari district.
  • Another Tamil Nadu wind region? → Kayathar.
  • Which gap helps channel winds into western Tamil Nadu? → Palghat Gap.
  • What is biomass? → Organic material used as an energy source.
  • What is biogas mainly composed of? → Methane and carbon dioxide.
  • How is biogas formed? → Anaerobic digestion.
  • What is bagasse? → Fibrous residue of sugarcane after juice extraction.
  • Bagasse is used for? → Cogeneration of heat and electricity.
  • What is cogeneration? → Simultaneous production of electricity and useful heat.
  • What is ethanol used for? → Fuel and petrol blending.
  • What is geothermal energy? → Heat from within Earth.
  • Important geothermal region of India? → Puga Valley, Ladakh.
  • Tidal-energy potential areas? → Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat.
  • What is OTEC? → Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion.
  • What does OTEC use? → Temperature difference between warm surface and cold deep ocean water.
  • Is hydrogen a primary energy resource? → No, it is an energy carrier.
  • What is green hydrogen? → Hydrogen produced by electrolysis using renewable electricity.
  • Commercial nuclear power mainly uses? → Nuclear fission.
  • The Sun produces energy by? → Nuclear fusion.
  • Important nuclear fuel? → Uranium.
  • Thorium is strongly associated with which mineral? → Monazite.
  • Monazite occurs mainly in? → Heavy-mineral coastal sands.
  • Important uranium centre in Jharkhand? → Jaduguda.
  • Important Tamil Nadu nuclear-energy centres? → Kalpakkam and Kudankulam.
  • Important Tamil Nadu hydroelectric region in Nilgiris? → Kundah.
  • Historic Nilgiri hydropower centre? → Pykara.
  • Important Tamil Nadu solar-energy location? → Kamuthi, Ramanathapuram.
  • What is energy efficiency? → Providing the same service with less energy.
  • What is energy security? → Reliable and affordable access to adequate energy.
  • Why is diversification of energy sources important? → It reduces dependence on any single source.
